lead: Differential pulse code modulation (DPCM) sends the difference between each sample and a prediction made from past samples, instead of the sample itself. Speech and most sensor signals change little from one sample to the next, so the difference is small and needs fewer bits for the same quality. The receiver adds the same prediction back. Adaptive DPCM (ADPCM) also adjusts the quantizer step to the signal’s short-term level; it carries telephone speech at 32 kbit/s, half the PCM rate.
prereq: You need: PCM and correlation between samples (see Random processes, stationarity, correlation and power spectral density).

blocks.text: Let x[n] be the sample at time index n, x̂[n] its prediction from earlier samples and x̃[n] the reconstructed sample that both ends can compute. DPCM quantizes the prediction error e[n] = x[n] − x̂[n] to q[n] and sends the level number as a code word of N bits, from L = 2ᴺ levels. The bit rate is N fs, the PCM formula with N bits for the difference. N can be smaller than the PCM word length because e[n] has a smaller spread than x[n].

blocks.where: The reconstructed sample differs from the input only by the quantization error of the difference: x[n] − x̃[n] = e[n] − q[n].

blocks.text: The simplest predictor uses the last reconstructed sample, x̂[n] = x̃[n − 1]. For a signal with variance σ² and correlation ρ between neighbouring samples, the error variance is then σ<sub>e</sub>² = 2σ²(1 − ρ). The best single-coefficient predictor x̂[n] = a x̃[n − 1] uses a = ρ and gives σ<sub>e</sub>² = σ²(1 − ρ²). Practical speech coders use several past samples.

sections.h3: Why the predictor sits inside the loop

blocks.text: The figure shows the transmitter and the receiver separately. The receiver has only q[n], so it can form only x̃. The transmitter therefore contains a copy of the receiver, its local decoder: it adds q[n] to x̂[n] to get x̃[n], and predicts the next sample from x̃, never from the true x.

items: Predict x̂[n] from stored reconstructed samples.
Quantize e[n] to q[n] and send its code.
Both ends add: x̃[n] = x̂[n] + q[n], and store it for the next prediction.

blocks.text: Because both predictors see the same x̃, they stay identical, and the error in each output sample is just one quantization error, e[n] − q[n]. If the transmitter predicted from x instead (open loop), the receiver’s predictions would drift away, and quantization errors would add up from sample to sample.

Gp is the prediction gain: the SQNR improvement over PCM with the same number of bits, since the quantizer now covers a range set by σe, not σ. With x̂[n] = x̃[n − 1] it is 10 log[1/(2(1 − ρ))]; each 6.02 dB of gain saves one bit.

The gain is not automatic. For ρ = 0.5 the simple predictor gives 0 dB, and for ρ = 0 it gives −3 dB: subtracting an unrelated sample doubles the variance. Telephone speech sampled at 8 kHz typically has ρ of about 0.85 to 0.9.

ADPCM makes the quantizer step Δ[n] follow the short-term level: loud passages get a large step to avoid overload, quiet ones a small step to cut granular noise. The step and often the predictor coefficients are computed from past code words, so the receiver tracks them with no side information. The ITU-T G.726 coder sends 4-bit differences at 8 kHz, 32 kbit/s. This is adaptation over time, not companding, which is a fixed curve.

examples.question: A signal has σ² = 1 V² and adjacent-sample correlation ρ = 0.9. Find the prediction-error variance and the prediction gain for x̂[n] = x̃[n − 1] and for the best coefficient a = ρ. About how many bits does DPCM save?
steps: Best coefficient: σ<sub>e</sub>² = σ²(1 − ρ²) = 1 − 0.81 = 0.19 V², so G<sub>p</sub> = 10 log<sub>10</sub>(1/0.19) = 7.21 dB.
Bits saved ≈ G<sub>p</sub>/6.02 = 6.99/6.02 = 1.16, so about one bit per sample.
examples.answer: σ<sub>e</sub>² = 0.2 V² and G<sub>p</sub> = 6.99 dB (0.19 V² and 7.21 dB with a = 0.9); DPCM saves about one bit per sample, 8 kbit/s at 8 kHz.

examples.question: A DPCM coder uses x̂[n] = x̃[n − 1], starts from x̃[−1] = 0, and quantizes e[n] with a 3-bit quantizer of step 0.5 V (levels ±0.25, ±0.75, ±1.25, ±1.75 V, codes 000 for −1.75 up to 111 for +1.75). Trace the inputs 1.1, 1.7, 2.2, 2.4, 2.1 and 1.4 V.
steps: Each later row repeats the same four steps, always predicting from x̃, so the receiver, which adds the same q[n], gets the same x̃ column.
Every output error is within ±0.25 V = ±Δ/2 although the input reaches 2.4 V, beyond the ±1.75 V quantizer range: the quantizer sees only differences.
examples.answer: Codes 110 100 101 100 011 010; reconstructed 1.25, 1.50, 2.25, 2.50, 2.25, 1.50 V; every error is within ±0.25 V.

traps: Both predictors must work from the reconstructed x̃, not the true x; predicting from x makes the receiver drift.
DPCM is not delta modulation: DPCM uses a multi-level quantizer; delta modulation is its 1-bit case (see Delta and adaptive delta modulation).
ADPCM adaptation is not companding: companding is a fixed curve, ADPCM changes the step with time.
With x̂[n] = x̃[n − 1] the gain is positive only for ρ > 0.5; at ρ = 0 it is −3 dB.

quiz.a: DPCM quantizes and sends the difference between each sample and a prediction formed from past reconstructed samples.

quiz.q: Why must the transmitter predict from x̃[n − 1] rather than x[n − 1]?
quiz.a: The receiver has only x̃. If the transmitter predicted from x, the two predictions would differ, and the receiver’s output would drift as quantization errors accumulate.

quiz.q: A source has σ² = 2 V² and ρ = 0.8. Find σ<sub>e</sub>² and G<sub>p</sub> for x̂[n] = x̃[n − 1].
ADPCM sends 4-bit differences at 8 kHz. Find the bit rate and the saving over 8-bit PCM.
quiz.a: 4 × 8000 = 32 kbit/s, half of 64 kbit/s, a saving of 32 kbit/s.

quiz.q: Explain how ADPCM reduces both overload and granular noise.
quiz.a: A large step in loud passages lets the quantizer cover big differences without clipping; a small step in quiet passages makes the rounding fine. The step is computed from past codes at both ends.

quiz.q: Show that the simple predictor helps only when ρ > 0.5.
quiz.a: G<sub>p</sub> = 10 log[1/(2(1 − ρ))] > 0 needs 2(1 − ρ) < 1, that is ρ > 0.5. At ρ = 0.5 the gain is 0 dB.

beyond: Not for the exam. Linear prediction with ten or more coefficients is the heart of modern speech coding (CELP), and lossless audio and image formats predict each sample from its neighbours before entropy coding. Search next for linear predictive coding and G.726.

spec.aria: Block diagram. Transmitter: x of n minus the prediction gives e of n, quantizer gives q of n, encoder sends the code; q of n plus the prediction gives the reconstructed sample, which feeds the predictor. Receiver: decoder gives q of n, which is added to the same prediction to give the reconstructed sample.
